title: No doubt in it
hookLine: a book for the mindful: those who believe in the unseen, pray, and give (2:2–3)
tomorrow: The one who lit a fire

cards: The Fatiha's last request is show us the straight path. Turn one page. Surah al-Baqarah opens with three Arabic letters, alif, lam, mim, whose meaning, most scholars say, God alone knows.

And then, as if answering the request just made, the second verse. In Pickthall's words: “This is the Scripture whereof there is no doubt, a guidance unto those who ward off (evil).” You asked for guidance.
Here it is. But notice who it says the guidance is for. Today: taqwa.

teach.b: Those who ward off evil. Pickthall's phrase translates one Arabic word: al-muttaqin, the people of taqwa. Taqwa comes from a root, w-q-y, meaning to guard, to shield yourself.
It gets translated as fear of God, piety, God-consciousness, mindfulness; each catches a piece. A story from the early commentaries, retold by Ibn Kathir, gives a picture.
Umar asked the companion Ubayy ibn Ka'b what taqwa is.
Ubayy asked him: have you ever walked a path full of thorns? Yes. And what did you do?
I gathered up my clothes and watched every step. That, said Ubayy, is taqwa. Not terror.

teach.h: THE UNSEEN, THE PRAYER, OPEN HANDS
teach.b: Verse three says what these mindful people look like: they believe in the unseen, they establish the prayer, and they spend from what they've been given. Trust in what you can't see.
A practice that keeps returning, five times a day. And open hands. Here's what stands out: the book says it's guidance for the mindful, not guidance that makes you mindful first and then guides you.
Many commentators read it as a loop.
A little attention lets you hear the book, and the book deepens the attention.
Look back at this week: a whole book opened, seven verses said seventeen times a day, a conversation where every line gets an answer, praise before asking. All of it was about attention.
Taqwa is the name for that attention, walking carefully through a thorny world with God in mind.

how: Muslims speak of taqwa as the aim of worship itself: the Qur'an names it as the purpose of fasting, and many say bismillah before ordinary acts to bring God to mind as they begin.

o: a special prayer said only late at night
mindfulness of God, like stepping carefully
terror of God's punishment, day and night

p: the root: to guard, to shield

s: taqwa only means being afraid of God
it's attention: guarding yourself, like walking carefully on a path of thorns.
al-Baqarah opens with three letters whose meaning most scholars leave to God
alif, lam, mim: some suggest meanings, many say only God knows.
verse three describes the mindful as those who pray and give
they believe in the unseen, establish the prayer and spend from what they're given.

games.q: Umar asks Ubayy ibn Ka'b what taqwa is. how does Ubayy answer?
o: with a definition from the Qur'an.
with a question about walking a thorny path.
games.why: a question: have you walked a path of thorns? you gather your clothes and watch every step. that's taqwa.

practice: Pick something small in front of you, a glass of water, standing up, your shoes, and do it slowly, the way you'd walk a path with thorns: the weight of the glass, the cold, the swallow. Then let the attention rest on your breath.
If you pray, you can say bismillah before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Taqwa. Mindfulness of God; from a root meaning to guard yourself, like gathering your clothes on a thorny path. The Qur'an calls itself guidance for the people of taqwa. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: mindfulness of God, from w-q-y, to guard or shield oneself; the people of taqwa are al-muttaqin.

carryVoice: Your line: guidance for the mindful. A little attention, and the book can be heard. Day three hundred thirty-six, and counting.

sources.q: This is the Scripture whereof there is no doubt, a guidance unto those who ward off (evil).

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:1 and 2:3 (alif lam mim; belief in the unseen, prayer, spending)
Tafsir Ibn Kathir on 2:2 (Umar and Ubayy ibn Ka'b on the thorny path)
